title: Milan Condemn Racist Abuse of Maignan After Bournemouth Red Card
excerpt: AC Milan said goalkeeper and captain Mike Maignan faced serious and unacceptable racist abuse on social media after his 27th-minute sending-off in the 3-0 Europa League defeat at Bournemouth.
body:
• AC Milan condemned racist abuse directed at goalkeeper and captain Mike Maignan on social media after his red card in a 3-0 Europa League defeat at Bournemouth on October 22.
  • Maignan was sent off in the 27th minute for pushing Bournemouth midfielder Tyler Adams in the face before a corner; Marcus Tavernier converted the resulting penalty.
  • Maignan said the gesture was not intentional, but Milan said the abuse that followed was serious and unacceptable and has no place on or off the pitch.
  • It is not the first time Maignan has faced racist abuse in Italy: in January 2024 he led his teammates off the pitch at Udine after being targeted from the stands.

AC Milan have condemned racist abuse aimed at their goalkeeper and captain, Mike Maignan, on social media following his sending-off in Thursday's 3-0 UEFA Europa League defeat at Bournemouth.

In an official statement published on Friday, the club said Maignan had been subjected to serious and unacceptable racist abuse after the fixture. Milan expressed full solidarity and support for the France international and reaffirmed a commitment to respect, inclusion and equality.

"AC Milan strongly condemns all forms of racism and discrimination, which are unacceptable and have no place either on or off the pitch."

— AC Milan, official statement

What happened at Bournemouth

Maignan was shown a red card in the 27th minute, according to Football Italia, for pushing Tyler Adams in the face as Bournemouth prepared to take a corner. Referee Vassilis Fotias sent the goalkeeper off, Marcus Tavernier converted the resulting penalty, and Bournemouth went on to win comfortably against 10 men, 3-0, in the League Phase match on October 22.

https://x.com/footballitalia/status/2113701772262850806

Maignan addressed the incident himself on social media on Friday. He said the gesture was not intentional and that he had been trying to create space inside his penalty area, while acknowledging that it created a poor image, particularly for younger supporters, and expressing regret at leaving his teammates a man short for more than an hour.

A familiar, unresolved problem

This is not an isolated episode for Maignan. In January 2024, he led his Milan teammates off the pitch at Udine after being targeted by racist abuse from the stands, briefly halting the match against Udinese. That incident prompted a wider debate in Italian football about sanctions, stadium closures and the protection of players.

The Bournemouth case differs in one respect: the abuse reported by Milan was online, on social media in the hours after the match, rather than from the stands. That distinction matters for enforcement. Clubs and leagues can identify spectators inside a stadium more readily than anonymous accounts online, which is why Milan's statement framed the response as a collective one rather than only a disciplinary one.

"We all want to win, but we need to win the right way with dignity, mutual respect and class."

— AC Milan, official statement

What Milan are asking for

The club appealed directly to its own supporters, including those frustrated by the result and by Maignan's red card. Milan said supporters and Italian football as a whole need to stand together, arguing that restoring Italian football depends on embracing dignity and mutual respect individually and collectively.

Criticism of a costly red card and abuse are not the same thing, and Milan's statement drew that line explicitly. Fans and pundits had widely questioned the captain's actions in the incident with Adams; the club did not dispute that scrutiny, but said racist insults crossed into discrimination that it would condemn without qualification.

What happens next

Maignan faces the sporting consequence of the red card through the normal Europa League disciplinary process, separate from the abuse case. Milan have not said in the statement whether specific accounts have been reported to the platforms or to authorities, and no sanction or investigation was announced in the material published on Friday.

For Milan, the immediate task is twofold: absorb the suspension of their captain and first-choice goalkeeper, and show that the solidarity in Friday's statement is followed by concrete reporting and action when abuse is identified. For European football, the episode is another test of whether online racist abuse after a high-profile mistake draws the same seriousness as abuse inside a stadium.
